---
title: "Bayes' rule"
---

The probability that a retained *ne* token is an object and the probability that a retained object token has lemma *ne* condition on different events. One cannot be read directly from the other.

The concrete denominator question is: should the 112 shared *ne*–object rows
be divided by all 147 *ne* rows, or by all 116 object rows? The answer depends
on which event appears to the right of the conditioning bar.

Bayes' rule follows by writing the same joint probability in the two possible
orders. The token counts then show exactly how the reversal changes the
denominator and why prevalence enters.

## Deriving Bayes' rule

Recall the two chain-rule factorizations:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)
=
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}(B,C)
=
\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

The left sides name the same intersection, so

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)\mathbb{P}(C)
=
\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B).
$$

If $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$, divide by $\mathbb{P}(C)$:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)\mathbb{P}(B)}
{\mathbb{P}(C)}.
$$

This identity is [**Bayes' rule**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html). It reverses the conditional direction while correcting for the two marginal probabilities. No independence assumption is used.

On the right side, $\mathbb{P}(C\mid B)$ is the conditional available in the
original direction, $\mathbb{P}(B)$ supplies the prevalence of the new target,
and $\mathbb{P}(C)$ changes the reference set to the new condition. The
numerator reconstructs $\mathbb{P}(B,C)$; the denominator then rescales that
joint mass within $C$.

```{r}
#| label: load-bayes-data
library(ggplot2)

wh <- read.csv(
  "data/ud-turkish-boun/question-core-arguments.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)

stopifnot(nrow(wh) == 167L)

is_ne <- as.logical(wh$ne_lemma)
is_object <- as.logical(wh$object)
p_ne <- mean(is_ne)
p_object <- mean(is_object)
p_object_given_ne <- mean(is_object[is_ne])
p_ne_given_object_direct <- mean(is_ne[is_object])
p_ne_given_object_bayes <- p_object_given_ne * p_ne / p_object

stopifnot(
  p_object > 0,
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    p_ne_given_object_direct,
    p_ne_given_object_bayes
  ))
)

c(object_given_ne = p_object_given_ne,
  ne = p_ne,
  object = p_object,
  ne_given_object = p_ne_given_object_bayes)
```

## Reversing the empirical conditional

Let $N$ be the *ne* event and $O$ the object event. Bayes' rule gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(N\mid O)
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(O\mid N)\mathbb{P}(N)}
{\mathbb{P}(O)}.
$$

The visible R calculation obtains `r round(p_ne_given_object_bayes, 3)`. Directly counting *ne* tokens among objects gives the same result, which verifies the identity against the raw rows.

```{r}
#| label: plot-bayes-directions
#| fig-cap: "The same joint count appears in both conditional directions, but each probability uses a different denominator."
conditional_directions <- data.frame(
  direction = c("obj among ne", "ne among obj"),
  probability = c(p_object_given_ne, p_ne_given_object_direct)
)

ggplot(conditional_directions,
       aes(direction, probability)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey65", width = 0.6) +
  geom_point(color = "#2C7FB8", size = 2.2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Conditional probability") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Evidence and prevalence

In this calculation, $\mathbb{P}(O\mid N)$ gives the object rate within *ne*, $\mathbb{P}(N)$ gives the prevalence of *ne* in the retained extract, and $\mathbb{P}(O)$ gives the overall object rate. All three quantities are tied to the same finite observation process.

The two conditionals may be numerically close or far apart depending on the margins. Their difference is not paradoxical: the shared intersection is divided once by the size of $N$ and once by the size of $O$. Reading the right side of the conditioning bar first identifies the denominator.

A potential worry is that the *ne* prevalence in this extract might be treated
as a population prevalence for Turkish. The source selected sentences from five
written registers, after which this analysis retained only three lemmas in two
dependency relations. Tokens contributed by the same sentence share local
context, and the register mixture does not represent the prevalence of registers
in Turkish production. Bayes' rule is exact for uniform sampling among these
retained rows; its inputs therefore describe this restricted table.

Bayes' rule is an algebraic reversal of two conditionals under one probability
measure. By itself it does not reverse a causal arrow or specify how the corpus
was sampled. Nor does it assign a distribution to a parameter: a [random
variable](../random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables.qmd) is a
mapping from outcomes to values, a concept introduced in the next module.

Reversing a conditional requires the original conditional and the relevant marginal probabilities. The [next page](independence.qmd) asks when conditioning leaves a probability unchanged.

## Check your understanding

1. Use Bayes' rule to compute $\mathbb{P}(L=\textit{kim}\mid O)$ from the reversed conditional and two margins.
2. Verify the result by filtering the raw object rows.
3. Explain why $\mathbb{P}(O\mid N)$ and $\mathbb{P}(N\mid O)$ share a numerator but not a denominator.
4. Which part of the calculation would change if the represented corpus deliberately oversampled one register?
5. A student calls $\mathbb{P}(N\mid O)$ the probability that being an object
   causes the lemma *ne*. Which unsupported step has been added?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. $\mathbb{P}(L=\textit{kim}\mid O)=\mathbb{P}(O\mid L=\textit{kim})\mathbb{P}(L=\textit{kim})/\mathbb{P}(O)=(3/17)(17/167)/(116/167)=3/116=0.025862$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Direct filtering finds 3 *kim* tokens among 116 object tokens, again giving $3/116=0.025862$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Both conditionals use the 112 *ne*–object tokens in the numerator; $\mathbb{P}(O\mid N)$ divides by 147 *ne* tokens, while $\mathbb{P}(N\mid O)$ divides by 116 object tokens. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Register oversampling would change the empirical margins and could also change the within-register mixture behind the conditional, so the Bayes calculation would need probabilities appropriate to the target register distribution. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. The conditional summarizes association under the empirical measure. A causal
   claim would require an intervention or a justified causal model, neither of
   which follows from algebraic reversal.

</details>

Bayes' rule works because the two directions of conditioning share a joint
numerator while using different margins as their denominators. The reversal
adds neither a causal claim nor a sampling claim. The [next
page](independence.qmd) asks when conditioning leaves a probability unchanged.
